summary: This unit teaches you to give each villa guest personal service: find out their likes and needs before and during the stay, record and share them, prepare the villa for them, arrange special occasions, care for guests with food allergies, diets or special needs, give personal services such as unpacking and beach set-ups, and protect their privacy. You will also learn how to say no politely and how to follow up.

blocks.p: Villa guests pay for something a large hotel cannot easily give: a stay that is shaped around them. A **customised** (personalised) service means you notice what each guest likes and needs, and you shape the service to fit. A guest who finds the pillow they like, the coffee they enjoy and a cook who knows about their allergy feels cared for, and tells friends and comes back.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees who work in villas, guest houses and small properties as hosts, butlers, housekeepers, cooks' helpers and guest service staff. It is about listening, remembering, preparing and being discreet.

What this means at the villa

Use pre-arrival forms and calls before the stay
Listen and observe during the stay
Ask politely, without being nosy

Keep a guest profile (history) and update it

Keep the profile private

Set up the room, the fridge and the welcome before arrival

Vegetarian, vegan, halal and kosher guests

Wheelchair users, older guests, guests who are hard of hearing
Families with babies and young children
Guests who speak little English
Give personal services
Unpacking and packing, pressing clothes, beach set-ups, picnics, turndown
Book massage, tours and chefs through approved suppliers
Protect privacy and handle limits
Be discreet; give no information about guests

Record in the guest profile
Prepare the villa and the team
Welcome by name
Notice and anticipate during the stay
Solve and follow up
Ask for feedback and update the profile

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks: you plan and set up a personalised arrival from a made-up guest profile, then set up a private patio dinner and handle personal service requests in role play. The assessor watches your planning, your attention to detail, your safety checks, your manner and your discretion.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work use made-up guest names and made-up profiles. A real guest's details are private and must never be shared or photographed.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Finding out what each guest likes and needs

ul: Guests who feel valued enjoy their stay more, spend more on extras, write good reviews and **come back**.
A villa has few guests and few staff, so it can know each guest personally. This is its greatest advantage.
Customised service costs little. Remembering a pillow or a favourite drink costs far less than the goodwill it earns.

head: When
How
Examples
rows: **Before arrival** (best time)
A pre-arrival form, email or phone call to the guest or the guest's agent.
Allergies, diet, arrival time, flights, pillows, room temperature, special occasions, who is travelling (children, older people), groceries to stock.
On arrival
The welcome conversation.
Confirm what you know, and ask 'Is there anything you would like us to change?'
During the stay
Listening and watching.
What the guest eats or leaves, how they use the room, what they ask for twice, what they say they love.
At departure
A short talk and a feedback form.
What they enjoyed and what to improve; whether they want to come again.

blocks.p: A good form is short and friendly. Questions that belong on it:

ul: Who is travelling (names, ages of children), and is anyone celebrating something?
Arrival time, flight or transport, and whether you should arrange a driver.
**Food allergies, dietary needs and dislikes.** Ask this on every form.
Pillow type, bed set-up (one king bed or two singles), room temperature, and anything needed for a baby (cot, high chair).
Mobility or other needs: steps, a ground-floor room, hearing or sight.
Favourite drinks, snacks and foods, to stock the kitchen.
Interests: beach, tours, reading, quiet time, children's activities.
Contact details, and how the guest likes to be contacted.

blocks.note: Ask only what you need to give better service. Do not ask about money, religion, health or family beyond what helps you serve. If the guest does not want to answer, accept that.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Reading the guest during the stay

ul: **Notice**: the guest takes the cushions to the patio; the child leaves the fruit; the guest is hot after a long walk.
**Ask politely**, when it suits: 'Would you like the air conditioning cooler tonight?' 'Do you prefer your coffee strong?'
**Check after a special service**: 'Was everything to your liking?' and watch their reaction as well as their words.
A guest who says very little may be shy or tired. Do not push. Offer, and let them choose.

blocks.p: A **guest profile** (or **guest history**) is a record of a guest's past stays and preferences. It lets any staff member give the guest the same personal service, even if they have not met before.

head: What goes in a profile
Example
rows: Name, title and how they like to be addressed
Dr Francis-Lewis; calls the host by first name.
Dates and rooms of past stays
Three stays; always Bedroom 2, with the sea view.
Preferences
Firm pillow, room at 22 °C, fresh coconut water at breakfast.
Allergies and diets (in a clearly marked place)
Egg allergy: no eggs in any dish or baked item.
Special dates
Birthday on 14 March; anniversary in July.
Complaints and how they were fixed
Noise from the road in 2023: moved to the back room.
Notes on service
Likes to be left alone in the mornings.

ul: Update it after every stay, and any time you learn something new. Record a favourite on the same day, before you forget.
**Only staff who need it to serve the guest** may see the profile. It is private. Do not share it outside the villa, or with other guests.
Pass it to the team at the **daily briefing**, so that every staff member gives the same personal service, not only the person who heard the guest say it.
Keep it where the property says: in a locked file or a password-protected system, never on a loose paper or an open phone.

blocks.note: Guest information is protected by data protection rules and by the villa's policy. Use it only to serve the guest. Never post about a guest, or put their details on social media, without their permission.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Preparing the villa for the guest

blocks.p: Customised service is mostly done **before the guest arrives**. When the guest walks in, they should find that the villa already knows them.

head: Area
What you prepare
rows: Bedrooms
The right bed set-up; the pillows the guest prefers (firm, soft, extra); a cot or extra bed if asked; the room cooled to the preferred temperature before they arrive.
Kitchen and fridge
The groceries, drinks and snacks the guest asked for; the favourite breakfast items; allergy-safe food kept apart.
Welcome
A note by name; a welcome drink; an amenity that matches the guest (see below).
Children and babies
Cot, high chair, socket covers, a baby gate if the villa has stairs or a pool; toys or books for the children.
Outdoor areas
Loungers, towels, an umbrella and cold water at the pool or beach; pool clean and safe; mosquito repellent if the guests like it.
Access needs
A clear step-free route, a ground-floor room, non-slip mats and a shower seat if requested.
Team
Cook, housekeeper and security told about the guest's names, arrival time, diet and plans at the briefing.

blocks.p: A guest may ask you to stock the fridge or buy items. Handle other people's money with great care.

flow: Agree a **shopping list**, a **budget** and **how the guest will pay**, in writing (an email or message is enough)
Buy exactly what is on the list, from a trusted shop; check dates and prices
Keep all **receipts**
Give the guest the receipts and any change, **counted out**, as soon as possible
Record it, and charge any fee the villa has agreed with the guest

ul: Never spend more than the budget without asking. Never buy a substitute for an allergy item without checking the label and asking the guest.
Never keep change, and never mix the guest's money with your own.
Greet a **returning guest** warmly by title and surname, thank them for coming back and offer a welcome drink. Say you have prepared the room as they like.
A guest who loves Blue Mountain coffee finds a handwritten note by name and a pot of it waiting. This is more personal than a general fruit basket.
If a guest says 'the usual' and you do not know what that is, check the profile, or ask kindly to be reminded. Never pretend to know.

blocks.note: Jamaican touches make a stay special: fresh fruit (mango, pineapple, June plum), Blue Mountain coffee, coconut water, a chilled welcome drink such as sorrel or ginger beer, and a handwritten welcome from the staff. Offer them as part of the villa's service, not as a way to sell more.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Villa guests often come to celebrate: an anniversary, a birthday, a honeymoon, a family reunion. Remembering the occasion and marking it well is one of the best ways to customise a stay.

flow: Find out about the occasion (before arrival if you can) and what the guest wants
Agree what you can offer, the **full cost** and how it will be paid, and get the guest's OK
Plan the timing, the place, the food (check allergies and diets) and the decoration
Check safety: weather, the tide, lighting, candles, steps, insects
Set up in good time, and check it again before the guests come
Serve quietly, then step away until called
Follow up, and record what went well in the profile

head: Occasion
Ideas the villa may offer (if its rules allow)
rows: Anniversary
A card, flowers or a small cake in the room on arrival; a private dinner for two on the patio or beach.
Birthday
A cake with candles, a card signed by the staff, a song, a decorated table.
Honeymoon
Flower petals on the bed, a bottle of sparkling drink, breakfast in bed, a couples' massage booked with an approved therapist.
Family reunion
A big table on the patio, a Jamaican meal, a group photo taken by staff.
Proposal
Only after the guest briefs you fully; you may be asked to help with the setting, and you must keep it secret.

ul: If a guest asks you to keep a surprise (a birthday for a husband, for example), **keep it secret** and help plan it. Do not mention it in front of the person it is for. Agree with the guest on how you will contact her privately (a phone message at a set time).
Brief every staff member, so that nobody lets it slip. Remind the team who must not hear about it.
Have a plan B, such as moving the setting indoors if it rains.

head: Detail
What to do
rows: Table
A steady table, a clean cloth, napkins, polished cutlery and glasses, with the places set neatly.
Decoration
Fresh flowers or leaves in a low vase; candles only in **glass holders**, or use battery candles, kept away from dry leaves, palm thatch and curtains.
Lighting
Soft but safe: you need to see steps and food; a torch is kept nearby.
Menu
A menu card matched to the guests' tastes; check each dish against any allergy.
Place
Quiet, private and level. On the beach, check the **weather, the tide and the lighting**: a rising tide, a strong wind or rain can ruin the dinner or be unsafe.
Comfort
Mosquito protection (a citronella candle in a holder, or a fan); chairs on firm sand or on boards.
Service
Serve from the left and clear from the right, as the villa's standard says, and step away. Come when called. Keep your voice low.

blocks.note: A **private chef** or other extra service usually costs extra. Before you book it, tell the guest the **full cost** and get their agreement. A surprise bill is a complaint waiting to happen.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Candles can start fires. Never leave a lit candle unattended near paper, dry leaves, thatch or curtains. Have water or an extinguisher close by when guests are outdoors.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Food is where customised service matters most, and where mistakes are most dangerous. A **food allergy** is the body's reaction to a food that can be mild (a rash) or life-threatening. The substance that causes it is an **allergen**.

blocks.h: A guest with a food allergy

flow: Ask about allergies on every pre-arrival form and at arrival
Record the allergy clearly in the profile and on the arrivals sheet
Tell the cook and every person who serves food, before the guest arrives
Check **every dish and snack**, including sauces, desserts and drinks, for the allergen
Keep food, utensils and boards for the allergic guest apart, to avoid **cross-contact**
Tell the guest what is in each dish when you serve it
Know what to do in an emergency

head: Common allergen
Where it hides
rows: Peanuts and tree nuts
Sauces, cakes and cookies, granola, some oils, curry mixes, ice cream.
Shellfish and fish
Stock, soups, sauces, seasoning blends; fried food cooked in oil used for shrimp.
Eggs and milk
Cakes, bread, batters, sauces, ice cream, chocolate.
Wheat (gluten)
Bread, dumplings, flour, soy sauce, many sauces and coating.
Soy and sesame
Sauces, bread, snacks, tofu.

ul: Read labels every time. Recipes and brands change.
Washing a pan does not always make it safe for an allergic guest. Use clean, separate equipment.
If you are not sure, **do not guess**. Say you will check, and ask the cook or the guest.

blocks.p: **Anaphylaxis** is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction. Signs: swelling of the lips, face or throat; trouble breathing; wheezing; a rash spreading fast; dizziness or fainting; vomiting.

flow: Call for help and ring the emergency number at once (in Jamaica, 110 for an ambulance; follow the villa's plan)
Ask whether the person has an adrenaline auto-injector and help them use it, if you are trained and they ask
Keep them still, sitting or lying as comfortable, and stay with them
Tell the ambulance and the supervisor exactly what the person ate
Write an incident report

blocks.note: Never wait to see whether a severe reaction goes away. Ring for help first.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Guest eats
What it means
Care points
rows: Vegetarian
No meat or fish. May eat eggs and milk.
A suitable Jamaican dish: ackee and callaloo with fried dumplings, or rice and peas cooked without meat or meat stock. Check soups and beans for meat or pork.
Vegan
No animal products at all: no meat, fish, eggs, milk or honey.
Cook with plant oil, not butter or ghee. Check bread, sauces and desserts. Ital food is plant-based, often cooked without salt.
Halal
Food allowed under Islamic rules: no pork, no alcohol, and meat from animals slaughtered in the halal way.
Check sauces and stock for pork and alcohol; keep pots and utensils separate; ask the guest what they accept.
Kosher
Food that follows Jewish food rules (for example no pork or shellfish, and meat and milk kept apart).
Ask the guest what they need; they may bring their own food or want a certified supplier.
Gluten-free, dairy-free or low-salt
For medical or personal reasons.
Read labels; prepare separately; ask whether it is an allergy or a preference.
Ital (Rastafari)
Natural, plant-based food, often without salt, meat, fish or alcohol.
Ask which rules the guest follows.

ul: Ask the guest what the diet means for them. Do not assume.
Treat every diet with respect, whether it is for health, religion or choice.
Tell the cook the exact rules, in writing.

blocks.note: Jamaican food gives plenty of choices: ackee and callaloo with dumplings, vegetable rundown, steamed vegetables with rice and peas, fruit platters, and a drink of sorrel at Christmas. A dish with salt fish, pork or chicken stock is **not** vegetarian. Check what is in it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every guest should enjoy the villa. Some need small changes to do so. Ask politely what would help and never assume what a person can or cannot do.

head: Guest
Before arrival
During the stay
rows: Uses a wheelchair or walking frame
Check the route from the gate to the bedroom, bathroom, dining area and pool for steps, narrow doors and rough ground
Offer a ground-floor room; set up a ramp if the villa has one
Move furniture to make space
Walk at their pace; do not push the wheelchair unless asked
Tell them about steps and wet floors
Offer a shower seat, non-slip mats and grab rails if available
Older guest, or a guest who finds stairs hard
Offer a room on the ground floor if one is free
Place a chair on the patio and a handrail where steps are
Offer an arm on steps and uneven paths
Keep walkways well lit
Hard of hearing
Note it in the profile
Face the guest and speak clearly, but do not shout
Offer to write things down
Check that they have heard instructions about safety
Low vision or blind
Note it; keep the room layout simple
Describe the room; keep things where they are; offer your arm and say what is ahead
Speaks little English
Ask the booking agent about language
Use simple words, gestures, pictures or a translation app
Write down times and names
Smile and be patient
Family with a baby or toddler
Prepare a cot, high chair, plug socket covers, a baby gate
Check that pool and stairs are safe
Show them what is safe and what is not
Offer a bottle warmer, a baby bath, and a babysitter from the villa's approved list
Guest from another culture
Learn about any customs you do not know
Respect them, and ask politely when you are unsure

ul: Do not make a guest feel different. Offer help as part of normal service.
If you do not know how to help, ask the guest or your supervisor.
Safety first: a hazard that a person without a disability would step over could injure a person with a disability.

blocks.p: To **anticipate** a need is to notice it and meet it **before the guest asks**. It is the sign of excellent service.

head: What you notice
What you do
rows: A guest comes back hot from a long walk in the sun
Offer a cold drink and a cool, damp face towel.
A guest takes a chair to the balcony
Leave it there, or place a comfortable balcony chair.
A child is sleepy after the beach
Offer to draw the curtains and bring a light blanket.
Rain is coming and the guests' clothes are on the line
Quietly bring them in.
Mosquitoes are biting at dusk
Offer repellent and light a citronella candle in a holder.
The guest mentions a favourite juice
Record it and have it at breakfast tomorrow.

ul: Ask the guest first how they like things put away. Handle items with care and respect, and never look through personal papers or belongings.
If you find **jewellery or valuables**, ask the guest where to put them, or suggest the safe. Never leave them out.
At departure, offer a packing service only if the guest wants it. Check drawers, bathroom and safe, and tell the guest what you find.
Never move or open anything locked or private.
Read the **care label** for the right iron setting before you press anything, especially silk and delicate fabrics.
If you are not sure that the garment can be pressed or washed safely, tell the guest and offer the alternative (a steamer, or a professional cleaner).
Return clothes on hangers, with the owner's name noted, as the villa's system says. Report damage honestly at once.

head: Service
What it includes
Check
rows: Beach set-up
Loungers, towels, an umbrella, cold water, and a shady spot.
Is the beach safe? Are the loungers clean and the umbrella firm?
Picnic basket
Food and drink packed for a beach or a waterfall, with plates, cups and napkins.
Allergies and diets; keep cold items cold; take the rubbish back.
Tours and activities
A boat trip, a river rafting trip, a hike, a driver.
Book **registered and approved** operators from the villa's list; give the guest the full cost; check the weather.
Massage and spa
A massage in the villa.
Book a **licensed therapist** from the approved list; check any health conditions and allergies; agree the cost first.
Turndown service
In the evening: bed folded back, lights dimmed, curtains drawn, a small treat.
Do it when the guests are out or when they have agreed, never when they are resting.
Private chef or butler
A chef who cooks the guests' meal, or a butler who attends to their personal needs.
Tell the guest the full cost and get their OK before you book.

blocks.p: **Discretion** means keeping quiet about guests' private matters and serving them without drawing attention. Guests at a villa live in a private home. They talk, argue, celebrate and relax. What you see and hear stays at the villa.

ul: **Serve quietly and step away** when guests are talking privately on the patio. Come when called.
Never discuss a guest with other guests, other staff who do not need to know, or friends and family outside work.
Do not post about guests, take photographs of them or share their names on social media.
If a reporter, a friend or a stranger phones to ask who is staying, say: 'I am sorry, I cannot say who is staying here.' This applies to famous guests too.
Do not enter the guests' private areas without a reason, unless invited or for an emergency.

blocks.note: If a guest offers to share a drink with you while you are on duty, thank them politely and say that you must stay on duty. It is not rude, and it protects you and the villa.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: You cannot always give a guest what they ask for. A request may be against the villa's rules, unsafe, illegal, impossible or too expensive. A polite 'no' with an alternative keeps the guest happy.

flow: Listen to the whole request and thank the guest for asking
Think: is it allowed, safe and possible?
If not, explain **kindly** and briefly why, without blaming the guest
Offer a **similar choice** that you can do
Tell your supervisor if the guest is still unhappy

head: Request
A good answer
rows: A party for far more people than the villa allows
Explain the villa's limit, and offer a smaller gathering or a table at a nearby venue.
A type of tea the local shops do not have
Explain, offer the nearest local choice such as fresh mint tea, and say you will try to have it next time.
The guest wants to swim alone late at night after drinking
Explain, kindly, that the villa asks guests not to swim alone at night, and offer to sit by the pool or arrange a daytime swim.
A request for an activity from an unlicensed operator
Explain that the villa uses only approved operators, and offer an approved one.
A guest asks you to keep something that is illegal quiet
Do not agree; tell your supervisor.

ul: Never promise what you cannot deliver, and never agree to something just to avoid an awkward moment.
Do not break the villa's rules for a guest, however polite or important the guest is.
If you do not know the answer, say you will find out and let them know soon, and then do so.

blocks.p: Suppose a guest's special request was forgotten and the guest is upset. This is how you recover:

flow: Say sorry sincerely and briefly
**Fix it fast**, even if it means a trip to the shop
Tell your supervisor what happened
Check that the guest is satisfied
Find out why it was forgotten and change the system (briefing, profile, checklist)

ul: **Ask** the guest politely whether a special service pleased them, and **watch** their reaction.
Give a **feedback form** or ask for comments at the end of the stay. This tells you what they liked and what to improve.
Record every new preference in the guest profile, and tell the team at the next briefing.
Good records bring guests back: a returning guest who finds their preferences remembered is likely to book again.
I can explain what customised guest service is and why villas offer it.
I can find out a guest's likes and needs before arrival, on arrival and during the stay.
I can write and use a pre-arrival form and a guest profile, and keep the profile private.
I can prepare a villa for a returning guest and for a family with young children.
I can shop for a guest with a list, a budget and receipts, and count the change.
I can plan a special occasion, keep a surprise and set up a safe private dinner.
I can deal safely with a food allergy, from the booking to the serving of the meal, and I know what to do in anaphylaxis.
I can serve vegetarian, vegan, halal and kosher guests with respect.
I can help guests who use a wheelchair, older guests, guests who are hard of hearing and guests who speak little English.
I can unpack, press and pack for a guest with care.
I can book massages, tours and chefs through approved suppliers and tell the guest the full cost.
I can anticipate needs, and I serve with discretion.
I can say no politely, offer an alternative and follow up on a mistake.
I can pass preferences to the team and ask for feedback.

terms: Customised service
Service shaped to each guest's own needs and likes.
Guest profile (history)
A record of a guest's past stays and preferences.
Preferences
A guest's likes and wishes, such as a firm pillow or a cool room.
Pre-arrival form
A short form or call to find out what a guest needs before the stay.
Amenity
A small welcome gift placed in a guest's room.
Anticipate
To notice and meet a need before the guest asks.
Discretion
Keeping private matters quiet and serving without drawing attention.
Allergen
A food or substance that can cause an allergic reaction.
Cross-contact
An allergen getting into another food, through equipment, hands or oil.
Anaphylaxis
A severe, life-threatening allergic reaction needing emergency help.
Vegetarian
A diet with no meat or fish.
Vegan
A diet with no animal products at all.
Halal
Food allowed under Islamic rules: no pork or alcohol.
Kosher
Food that follows Jewish food rules.
Ital
A natural, plant-based way of eating in the Rastafari tradition.
Ramp
A sloping path used instead of steps, for wheelchairs.
Butler
A staff member who looks after guests' personal needs, such as unpacking and serving.
Turndown service
An evening service: bed folded back, lights dimmed, curtains drawn.
Upselling
Suggesting a better or extra service when it suits the guest.
Feedback form
A form where a guest tells you what they liked and what to improve.

c1.title: Dr Francis-Lewis returns to Treasure Beach
c1.text: Dr Marcia Francis-Lewis and her husband are coming back for their fourth stay at a villa in Treasure Beach. Their profile says: extra-firm pillows, bedroom cooled to 22 °C, fresh coconut water at breakfast, and an allergy to eggs. They have emailed asking for the fridge to be stocked with a list of items and a budget of J$25,000. Host Roshane is preparing for their arrival the next afternoon.

c2.title: A surprise birthday on the deck
c2.text: Ms Kerisha Ellis is staying with her husband, Garth, at a villa in Ocho Rios. She asks host Andre in private to arrange a surprise dinner for Garth's 40th birthday on the deck on Friday evening, with a cake and candles. The deck has a palm-thatch roof and a rail covered in dry vines. Garth is allergic to prawns. The villa's cook has not yet been told.

c3.title: Three diets at one table
c3.text: The Mohammed family from Toronto are staying at a villa in Negril: two adults, a teenager who is vegan, a grandmother who eats only halal food, and a boy aged 6 with a peanut allergy. The cook, Miss Joyce, suggests ackee and saltfish with fried dumplings, callaloo with rice and peas, and a peanut-butter cookie for the boy's snack. The family arrives tomorrow.

c4.title: Mr and Mrs Thomas at a hillside villa
c4.text: Mr Aubrey Thomas, 78, uses a walking frame, and his wife, 75, is hard of hearing. They are booked into a hillside villa in Mandeville. The master bedroom is upstairs. A ground-floor bedroom has a shower with a high step. The path from the car park to the front door has three steps and a ramp at the side. Housekeeper Lorna is preparing for them.

c5.title: Requests from Mr Bennett
c5.text: Mr Garfield Bennett, a guest at a villa in Port Antonio, asks housekeeper Tameka to unpack his suitcase and to press a silk shirt. While unpacking she finds a gold watch and some cash in a shirt pocket. Later he asks her to book a massage for his wife in the villa this afternoon with a woman he met on the beach.

c6.title: A guest who values her privacy
c6.text: A well-known musician is staying at a villa in Treasure Beach with her family. A friend of staff member Dwight sends him a message asking for a photo of her at the pool and whether it is true that she is there. That evening the musician asks for a quiet dinner on the patio and says she wants to be left alone afterwards. The next morning she tells Dwight she likes to sleep late in a dark, quiet room, so nobody should knock before 9:00 a.m.

questions.q: What should Roshane do about Dr Francis-Lewis's egg allergy?
o: Tell Dr Francis-Lewis to ask for egg-free food herself
Avoid cooking eggs on the day she arrives, and then carry on as usual
Tell the cook and check every dish and baked item for egg
Put a note on the fridge and leave the menu to the cook
questions.why: An allergy must be passed to everyone who prepares or serves food, and every dish, sauce and baked item must be checked. A note on the fridge or reliance on the guest is not safe.

questions.q: At the shop the groceries on the list come to J$27,400, which is J$2,400 over the budget. What should Roshane do?
o: Leave out the J$2,400 worth of items he thinks she will not really miss
Buy cheaper brands of everything on the list so that the total fits her budget
Buy everything, and add the extra amount to the villa's own costs this week
Message Dr Francis-Lewis and ask what to cut or if she agrees
questions.why: Never spend over an agreed budget without asking. Tell the guest, and let her decide what to remove or whether to pay more. Changing the list yourself or hiding the difference is not honest service.

questions.q: Roshane was given J$25,000 in cash and the receipts add up to J$22,650. What should he give Dr Francis-Lewis?
o: The receipts and J$2,650 in change, rounded up for her
The receipts and J$2,350 in change, counted out
J$2,350 in change, and throw away the receipts to save paper
The receipts only, and keep the change for the next shopping trip
questions.why: 25,000 − 22,650 = J$2,350. A guest gets back every receipt and the exact change, counted out in front of her. Never keep change or mix a guest's money with your own.

questions.q: One loaf at the shop lists egg among its ingredients. What should Roshane do?
o: Buy it anyway, because only a little egg is in each slice of the bread
Choose a loaf with no egg, after reading its label
Buy it, and cut off the crust, as the egg is mainly in the middle of it
Buy it, and tell the cook not to serve it to Dr Francis-Lewis herself
questions.why: A guest with an egg allergy must not be served food that contains egg, even a small amount. Read every label, and choose a product with no egg.

questions.q: Ms Ellis wants candles on the cake and on the deck table. What is the safest plan?
o: Use battery candles on the table, and a cake candle held while it is lit
Light only one candle on the table, and keep it away from the guests
Put real candles around the deck rail, and keep a bucket of water by the thatch
Light candles in paper cups so that they are easy to carry out
questions.why: Dry thatch and vines catch fire easily. Use battery candles or glass holders well away from them, and light a cake candle only while it is in someone's hands. Never leave a flame unattended.

questions.q: How should Andre keep the surprise from Garth?
o: Tell every member of staff, so that nobody is surprised by the work being done
Ask Garth for a different time, so that the surprise is easier to plan
Put the decorations up on the deck the morning before the dinner
Brief only the staff who need to know, and contact her privately
questions.why: A surprise is kept by briefing only those staff who must know, and by agreeing a private way to reach the guest. Visible preparations, or asking the person it is for, spoil it.

questions.q: What should Andre do about Garth's prawn allergy?
o: Leave prawns off the menu, but do not tell the cook the reason why
Ask Garth at the dinner table whether the food is all right for him
Serve the food as planned, and tell Garth what is in each dish as it comes
Tell the cook now, and check every dish and the cake
questions.why: The cook must know about the allergy before planning the menu. Every dish, including sauces and the cake, must be checked in advance. Asking at the table is too late.

questions.q: Which of Miss Joyce's suggestions should be changed for the boy?
o: The peanut-butter cookie, which contains peanuts
The fried dumplings, which are made with flour
The rice and peas, which are cooked in coconut milk
The callaloo, which is a leafy green vegetable
questions.why: Peanut butter is peanut, the boy's allergen, so the cookie must go. The other dishes do not contain peanuts, though labels and oils should still be checked.

questions.q: Which suggested dish could suit the vegan teenager, after checking?
o: Rice and peas, which the cook flavours with a piece of salted pigtail
Fried dumplings, which the cook will fry in the same oil as the saltfish
Ackee and saltfish, because ackee is a fruit and not an animal product
Callaloo and rice and peas, with plant oil and no meat or stock
questions.why: Vegan food has no animal products. Callaloo and rice and peas can be vegan if made without meat, stock or butter. Saltfish is fish, and pork or shared frying oil is not acceptable.

questions.q: What is the most important check for the grandmother's meals?
o: No pork or alcohol in any dish, including stock and seasoning
Her meals are cooked last of all, after the vegan teenager's meals
Her meals are served cold, to be certain that they are fresh and safe
Her meals are served on plates that are kept apart from the others at table
questions.why: Halal food excludes pork and alcohol, and these can hide in stock, sauces and seasoning. Callaloo is sometimes cooked with salted meat, so check. Ask her what she accepts.

questions.q: During the stay the boy gets swollen lips and wheezes after a snack. What should the host do first?
o: Take him to the room to lie down, and check on him later
Call an ambulance and use his auto-injector if he has one
Give him a glass of water, and watch to see how he gets on
Phone his parents in town, and wait for them to decide
questions.why: Swelling and wheezing after a food are signs of anaphylaxis, which can kill quickly. Ring for emergency help at once, and use his adrenaline auto-injector if he has one. Never wait to see whether it passes.

questions.q: Where should Lorna put Mr and Mrs Thomas?
o: The master bedroom, since it is the best room in the villa
The ground-floor bedroom, with a shower seat and a non-slip mat
The master bedroom, with a chair on the stairs for resting
The ground-floor bedroom, and tell them to take care in the shower
questions.why: Stairs are a risk for a walking-frame user, so the ground-floor room is the better choice. The high shower step is a hazard, so make it safer with a seat and a non-slip mat, and tell the guests.

questions.q: How should Lorna deal with the path from the car park to the front door?
o: Leave it as it is, since guests can see the way to the door for themselves
Ask him to use the three steps, with Lorna's arm for support all the way
Keep the ramp clear and lit, and show him the easiest way
Move the car park to the other side of the villa, where the ground is flat
questions.why: Steps are hard for someone with a walking frame, so show the ramp and keep it clear and lit. Offering a better route is part of preparing for a guest's needs.

questions.q: What is the best way for Lorna to speak with Mrs Thomas about the evening meal and the alarm?
o: Face her, speak clearly, and write down times and instructions
Say it quickly just the once, and walk away before she asks any questions
Speak loudly from across the room, so that she hears over any noise
Tell Mr Thomas the details, and let him pass them on to his wife
questions.why: Face a person who is hard of hearing, speak clearly (not loudly) and offer written notes. Check that she has understood the safety instructions, which are the most important.

questions.q: The care label on Mr Bennett's silk shirt says 'dry clean only'. What should Tameka do?
o: Press it on the lowest setting, with a damp cloth over the silk
Press it on the highest setting, to be sure the creases come out
Tell him, and offer a dry cleaner rather than pressing it
Wash it by hand, and press it while it is still damp
questions.why: When the care label says dry clean only, do not iron or wash the shirt. Tell the guest and offer a dry cleaner or another safe way. Pressing silk at the wrong heat can ruin it, and the villa would be responsible.

questions.q: What should Tameka do about the gold watch and cash she finds?
o: Take them to the owner's office for safe-keeping until the guest asks
Leave them in the pocket and say nothing, to avoid any possible trouble
Put them in the dressing-table drawer without telling anyone about them
Tell Mr Bennett where she found them, and ask where to keep them
questions.why: Valuables found while unpacking are shown to the guest, who decides where to put them, perhaps in the safe. Hiding them or taking them without his say-so could cause a loss or an accusation.

questions.q: How should Tameka answer the massage request?
o: Book the woman Mr Bennett met, since he has chosen her himself
Offer a licensed therapist from the approved list
Give him a phone number for the woman, and let him arrange it
Say that no massages are possible at a private villa like this one
questions.why: The villa uses only licensed, approved therapists, for the guests' safety and the villa's. Explain kindly and offer a good alternative, rather than refusing or letting an unknown person into the house.

questions.q: How should Dwight answer his friend's message?
o: Send a photo from far away, so that her face is not seen
Say she is there, and ask the friend to keep it quiet
Confirm that she is there, but send no photo
Say he cannot say who is staying, and send no photo
questions.why: Guests' presence and privacy are never shared, whoever they are. Do not confirm, deny or photograph. A polite refusal protects the guest and the villa.

questions.q: How should the staff serve the musician's quiet patio dinner?
o: Ask her questions about her work as you serve
Stay by the table to be ready for any request
Serve quietly, then step away and come when called
Serve all the courses at once, so that nobody needs to return
questions.why: Discretion means serving without intruding. Step away and let the guest enjoy her privacy, but stay near enough to answer when she calls. Personal questions are not appropriate.

questions.q: What should Dwight do with her request to sleep late in a quiet room?
o: Remember it himself and tell nobody else, to protect her privacy
Tell housekeeping to clean her room before she wakes up each day
Record it in her profile and tell housekeeping
Ask her to put out a Do Not Disturb sign each night before bed
questions.why: A preference must be recorded and shared, so every staff member respects it, for example by not knocking before 9:00 a.m. Keeping it in your own head means the next shift will disturb her.
